mainTopic: The order of שמונה עשרה, limits on praising God, and the laws of reading the מגילה (by heart, in translation, in other languages, and with breaks)
overview: The amud opens by finishing the גמרא's explanation of the order of שמונה עשרה. Each blessing is linked to the next by a פסוק: דוד, then תפלה, עבודה, הודאה, ברכת כהנים and שים שלום. The גמרא explains that the 120 elders set the order, it was later forgotten, and שמעון הפקולי restored it. One may not add praises of God beyond these fixed blessings, and silence is the best praise. The גמרא then returns to the משנה about reading the מגילה. רבא learns from עמלק that it must be read from a written text, and a ברייתא shows the words must be said aloud. Any language works for people who speak it, and רב ושמואל add that Greek works for everyone, following רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. A לועז who hears the Hebrew is יוצא, because the מצוה is the reading and פרסומי ניסא. The amud ends with stories of how the רבנן learned rare words like סירוגין from everyday speech, and the start of a ברייתא that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Verse showing דוד's kingdom comes with the return to ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its proof that the blessing for מלכות בית דוד follows the blessing for building ירושלים. It quotes a פסוק from הושע about the return to ה׳ and to דוד their king.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Afterward the children of Israel shall return, and seek ה׳ their God and דוד their king."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a proof that started on the previous amud. It explains why the blessing about דוד's kingdom comes right after the blessing about rebuilding ירושלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the Jewish people return and seek ה׳ in a rebuilt ירושלים, they will also seek דוד their king. So in שמונה עשרה, the blessing for בית דוד (את צמח דוד) is placed right after the blessing for building ירושלים (בונה ירושלים).

keyTerms.meaning: They will return (do תשובה / come back)
David their king, meaning the kingdom of the house of David

steps.confusionAlert: This amud begins in the middle of a sugya. The verse here is the proof for a step that started on the previous עמוד (why דוד follows ירושלים). It is not a brand-new topic.

phrases.english: "Afterward the children of Israel shall return
phrases.notes: הושע ג:ה

phrases.english: and seek ה׳ their God
and David their king."
phrases.notes: Seeking ה׳ (in ירושלים) is paired with seeking דוד, so דוד's blessing follows ירושלים.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַחַר יָשׁוּבוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבִקְשׁוּ אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֵיהֶם וְאֵת דָּוִד מַלְכָּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the derivation begun on the previous amud (ירושלים → דוד).
steps.raayaObject: The placement of the blessing for מלכות בית דוד right after בונה ירושלים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: הושע ג:ה — 'Afterward the children of Israel shall return… and David their king.'

steps.title: Once דוד comes, prayer comes
steps.stepSummary: The blessing שומע תפלה follows the blessing for דוד. The proof is ישעיה's promise that ה׳ will bring the people to His holy mountain and make them joyful in His house of prayer.
steps.simpleTranslation: And once דוד comes, prayer comes, as it says: "I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next link in the chain. It explains why שומע תפלה comes right after the blessing for דוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the time of redemption under דוד's kingdom, the בית המקדש will be a 'house of prayer.' So after asking for דוד's kingdom, we ask ה׳ to hear our prayers.

keyTerms.meaning: And once [X] comes (the linking formula of this chain)
Prayer; here, the blessing שׁוֹמֵעַ תְּפִלָּה
My house of prayer (the בית המקדש)

phrases.english: And once David comes —
prayer comes, as it is stated:
"I will bring them to My holy mountain
phrases.notes: ישעיה נו:ז

phrases.english: and make them joyful in My house of prayer."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next link in the chain: דוד → תפלה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שומע תפלה is placed right after the blessing for מלכות בית דוד.

steps.title: Once prayer comes, the Temple service comes
steps.stepSummary: The blessing for restoring the עבודה (רצה) follows שומע תפלה. The proof is the continuation of the same פסוק in ישעיה, about offerings accepted on ה׳'s altar.
steps.simpleTranslation: And once prayer comes, the Temple service comes, as it says: "Their burnt-offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted on My altar."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds the next link. It explains why the blessing for the Temple service comes after the blessing for prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same פסוק that mentions the 'house of prayer' goes on to speak of sacrifices accepted on the altar. So the order in the verse, prayer first and then sacrifices, becomes the order of the blessings.

keyTerms.meaning: The Temple service; here, the blessing רְצֵה

phrases.english: And once prayer comes —
the Temple service comes, as it is stated:
"Their burnt-offerings and their sacrifices
phrases.notes: Continuation of ישעיה נו:ז

phrases.english: shall be accepted on My altar."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next link in the chain: תפלה → עבודה, using the second half of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The blessing רצה (restoration of the עבודה) follows שומע תפלה.

steps.title: Once the service comes, thanksgiving comes
steps.stepSummary: The blessing of הודאה (מודים) follows the blessing for עבודה. The proof is from תהלים: 'One who offers a thanksgiving-offering honors Me.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And once the Temple service comes, thanksgiving comes, as it says: "Whoever sacrifices a thanksgiving-offering honors Me."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds the last link of this chain. It explains why מודים comes right after רצה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק links a sacrifice (זוֹבֵחַ) with thanksgiving (תּוֹדָה). This shows that thanks comes along with the sacrificial service, so מודים is placed directly after the blessing for the עבודה.
steps.whatToRemember: The chain so far: ירושלים → דוד → תפלה → עבודה → הודאה. Each link is supported by a פסוק that places the second thing right after the first.

phrases.english: And once the Temple service comes —
thanksgiving comes, as it is stated:
"Whoever sacrifices a thanksgiving-offering honors Me."
phrases.notes: תהלים נ:כג

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final link in the chain: עבודה → הודאה.

steps.title: Why is the Priestly Blessing placed after thanksgiving?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why ברכת כהנים was instituted to be said right after the blessing of הודאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why did they see fit to say the Priestly Blessing after thanksgiving?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question about the next piece of the תפלה. It is setting up the proof that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The chain so far linked one blessing to the next. Now the גמרא wants a reason for placing ברכת כהנים, which the חזן says in חזרת הש״ץ, right after מודים.

keyTerms.meaning: And what did they see (i.e., what reason did the Sages have) to…

phrases.english: And why did they see fit to say
the Priestly Blessing after thanksgiving?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמָה רָאוּ לוֹמַר בִּרְכַּת כֹּהֲנִים אַחַר הוֹדָאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the chain of linked blessings to the placement of ברכת כהנים.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source or reason for placing ברכת כהנים after הודאה.

steps.title: Aaron blessed the people after the sacrifices
steps.stepSummary: The answer comes from ויקרא: אהרן lifted his hands and blessed the people, and came down from offering the חטאת, עולה and שלמים. This shows that the blessing came after the sacrificial service, and the תודה is part of that service.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: "And אהרן lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them, and he came down from offering the sin-offering, the burnt-offering and the peace-offerings."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a פסוק about אהרן's first day of service in the משכן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אהרן blessed the people in connection with finishing the sacrifices. Since עבודה and הודאה (the תודה offering) belong together as the sacrificial service, ברכת כהנים follows that whole unit, which means it comes right after מודים.

keyTerms.meaning: And אהרן lifted his hands (the gesture of ברכת כהנים)

phrases.english: As it is written: "And Aaron lifted his hands
phrases.notes: ויקרא ט:כב

phrases.english: toward the people and blessed them
and he came down from offering the sin-offering
and the burnt-offering and the peace-offerings."

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב וַיִּשָּׂא אַהֲרֹן אֶת יָדָיו אֶל הָעָם וַיְבָרְכֵם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ברכת כהנים follows the sacrificial service, as seen from אהרן's blessing after the offerings.

steps.title: Maybe the Priestly Blessing should come before the service
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the reading. In the פסוק, 'he blessed them' appears before 'he came down… the sin-offering.' Maybe that means the blessing came first, and ברכת כהנים should be placed before the blessing of עבודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: before the Temple service?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof just given. It suggests the verse might put the blessing before the sacrifices.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the verse, the words order the blessing (וַיְבָרְכֵם) ahead of the mention of the offerings. If the blessing came first, the proof would flip, and ברכת כהנים would belong before רצה, not after מודים.

phrases.english: Say instead: before the Temple service?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof of step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof from ויקרא ט:כב that ברכת כהנים comes after the עבודה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse mentions the blessing before the offerings, so maybe the blessing came first and should be said before רצה.

steps.title: The verse says 'from offering,' meaning the sacrifices were already done
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the challenge. The פסוק says מֵעֲשׂוֹת ('from having done'), not לַעֲשׂוֹת ('to do'). So the sacrifices were already finished when אהרן blessed the people, and ברכת כהנים comes after the עבודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't think that, as it is written: "And he came down from offering the sin-offering." Is it written 'to offer'? It is written 'from offering.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by looking closely at one word in the פסוק. This confirms its original answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: לַעֲשׂוֹת would mean he came down to go offer the sacrifices, which would put the blessing first. מֵעֲשׂוֹת means he came down after finishing them. So the blessing followed the service, and the original placement after עבודה and הודאה stands.

keyTerms.meaning: It should not enter your mind (don't think that)
Is it written…? (rhetorical: it is not)
To do / to offer (still to come)
From doing / from having offered (already finished)

steps.whatToRemember: ברכת כהנים comes after עבודה and הודאה because אהרן blessed the people after he finished the sacrifices. The proof is the word מֵעֲשׂוֹת ('from having done'), not לַעֲשׂוֹת ('to do').
steps.confusionAlert: Don't be misled by the word order of the פסוק. Even though 'he blessed them' is written before the offerings are mentioned, the word מֵעֲשׂוֹת shows the offerings were already completed.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the חזן says ברכת כהנים (and why כהנים go up to bless) after מודים, near the end of שמונה עשרה, and not earlier in the עבודה section.

phrases.english: It should not enter your mind,
as it is written: "And he came down from offering the sin-offering, etc."
Is it written 'to offer'?
'From offering' is written.
phrases.notes: The sacrifices were already completed before the blessing.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ דִּכְתִיב וַיֵּרֶד מֵעֲשׂוֹת הַחַטָּאת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the challenge of step 7 and upholds the answer of step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Precise reading of a word in the פסוק (מֵעֲשׂוֹת vs. לַעֲשׂוֹת).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The blessing came before the offerings, so ברכת כהנים belongs before רצה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The offerings were already finished (מֵעֲשׂוֹת), so ברכת כהנים comes after the עבודה and הודאה.

steps.title: Shouldn't the Priestly Blessing come right after the Temple-service blessing?
steps.stepSummary: If ברכת כהנים follows the sacrificial service, it should be placed right after the blessing of עבודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it be said right after the blessing of עבודה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the order we just learned. If ברכת כהנים comes after the service, why not place it directly after עבודה, before מודים?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 proved that אהרן blessed the people after finishing the sacrifices. Taken by itself, that proof suggests ברכת כהנים should sit right next to עבודה. Here, הודאה looks like an interruption.

keyTerms.meaning: After the blessing of the Temple service (רצה)

phrases.english: So let it (ברכת כהנים) be said right after the blessing of the service!
phrases.notes: Without מודים in between.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the conclusion of step 8 to challenge where הודאה is placed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The placement of הודאה between עבודה and ברכת כהנים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If ברכת כהנים follows the service, nothing should separate it from the blessing of עבודה.

steps.title: No, because thanksgiving goes with sacrifice
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק 'זובח תודה' links thanksgiving directly to sacrifice, so הודאה must come right after עבודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't think that, because it is written: 'One who sacrifices a thanksgiving-offering.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the challenge. It uses the same פסוק from step 4: thanksgiving belongs right next to sacrifice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse 'זובח תודה יכבדנני' joins sacrifice and thanks into one act. So הודאה gets the spot right after עבודה, and ברכת כהנים comes after both.

keyTerms.meaning: It should not enter your mind (that idea is rejected)

phrases.english: It should not enter your mind,
as it is written: 'One who sacrifices a thanksgiving-offering.'
phrases.notes: תהלים נ:כג, the same verse used in step 4.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9 by pointing back to the verse from step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Appeal to a verse that links sacrifice and thanks
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ברכת כהנים should follow עבודה immediately.
steps.terutzMaskana: הודאה is tied to sacrifice by 'זובח תודה', so it comes first.

steps.title: Why rely on this verse and not the other one?
steps.stepSummary: Both verses seem to claim the spot after עבודה. Why does the תודה verse win over the ויקרא verse?
steps.simpleTranslation: What did you see that made you rely on this verse? Rely on that one instead!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a tie. One verse puts thanks next to sacrifice, and the other puts the priestly blessing next to sacrifice. Why does thanks win?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only one blessing can sit right after עבודה. Both the תהלים verse and the ויקרא verse could claim that spot. The גמרא demands a reason to prefer one.

keyTerms.meaning: What did you see? (Why choose this option over the other?)

phrases.english: What did you see that you relied on this verse (זובח תודה),
rely on that verse (the one about אהרן's blessing)!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 10's choice of verse.
steps.kashyaTarget: Why the תודה verse is preferred over the ויקרא verse.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two verses compete for the same spot, and no reason has yet been given to prefer one.

steps.title: Logic: service and thanksgiving are one thing
steps.stepSummary: It makes sense that הודאה goes with עבודה, because they are really one idea.
steps.simpleTranslation: It stands to reason: the service and thanksgiving are one matter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא breaks the tie with simple logic. Thanking God and serving God through sacrifice belong together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse alone did not decide the question, so a logical point does. עבודה and הודאה are one idea (a תודה is itself a sacrifice). ברכת כהנים is a separate thing that comes after the whole service.

keyTerms.meaning: It stands to reason / it makes sense

steps.whatToRemember: Order: עבודה, then הודאה (they are one idea), then ברכת כהנים (after the service is complete).

phrases.english: It stands to reason
the service and thanksgiving are one matter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the tie raised in step 11.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Either verse could claim the spot after עבודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: הודאה wins because it is part of the same idea as עבודה.

steps.title: Why does 'Grant Peace' come after the Priestly Blessing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of placing שים שלום after ברכת כהנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why did they decide to say 'שים שלום' after ברכת כהנים?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the last blessing of the עמידה and asks why it was placed right after ברכת כהנים. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the pattern of explaining the reason for each blessing's position. The question is not an attack. It simply asks for the source.

keyTerms.meaning: And why did they see fit (to set it up this way)
'Grant peace', the final blessing of the עמידה

phrases.english: And why did they see fit to say 'Grant peace'
after the Priestly Blessing?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next blessing in the sequence, following the same pattern as step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for placing שים שלום after ברכת כהנים.

steps.title: God's blessing that follows the כהנים is peace
steps.stepSummary: After ברכת כהנים the Torah says 'and I will bless them,' and God's blessing is peace. So the blessing of peace follows ברכת כהנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'They shall place My name on the children of Israel, and I will bless them.' The blessing of the הקב"ה is peace, as it says: 'ה׳ will bless His people with peace.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with two פסוקים. Right after ברכת כהנים God promises to bless, and God's blessing is peace. So the peace blessing comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first verse (במדבר ו:כז) shows that God's own blessing follows the כהנים' blessing. The second verse (תהלים כט:יא) defines that blessing as peace. Together they explain why שים שלום comes right after ברכת כהנים.

keyTerms.meaning: They shall place My name (the end of ברכת כהנים in the תורה)
He will bless His people with peace

steps.whatToRemember: Full order of the end of the עמידה: עבודה, הודאה, ברכת כהנים, שים שלום.

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְתִיב: ״וְשָׂמוּ אֶת שְׁמִי עַל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
phrases.english: As it is written: 'And they shall place My name upon the children of Israel
phrases.notes: במדבר ו:כז, right after ברכת כהנים.

phrases.english: and I will bless them,'
and the blessing of the Holy One, Blessed be He, is peace,
as it is stated: 'ה׳ will bless His people with peace.'
phrases.notes: תהלים כט:יא

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: ״וְשָׂמוּ אֶת שְׁמִי עַל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וַאֲנִי אֲבָרְכֵם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: God's blessing follows ברכת כהנים, and that blessing is peace, so שים שלום comes next.

steps.title: If the 120 elders set the order, what did שמעון הפקולי arrange?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says 120 elders, including prophets, set the order of the תפילה. So what did שמעון הפקולי add?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, since 120 elders, among them many prophets, established the תפילה in its order, what did שמעון הפקולי arrange?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the opening sources of the sugya and points out a contradiction. Two sources seem to credit different people with arranging the same prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One source, taught by רבי יוחנן (and some say in a ברייתא), says the 120 elders of the אנשי כנסת הגדולה fixed the order of the blessings. Another ברייתא says שמעון הפקולי arranged them much later, in front of רבן גמליאל in יבנה. If the order was already fixed, his work seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: The sage who arranged the blessings before רבן גמליאל in יבנה

phrases.english: Now, since 120 elders,
and among them many prophets,
established the prayer in its order,
what did שמעון הפקולי arrange?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the order-of-blessings discussion and returns to the sources that opened the sugya.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that שמעון הפקולי arranged the blessings.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The order was already fixed by the 120 elders, so there was nothing left for him to arrange.

steps.title: The order was forgotten, and he restored it
steps.stepSummary: Over time the order was forgotten, and שמעון הפקולי set it up again.
steps.simpleTranslation: They forgot them, and he went back and arranged them again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction. Both sources are true: the elders set the order first, and שמעון הפקולי restored it after it was forgotten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two sources describe two different moments in history. The original setting of the order and its later restoration do not contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: And he went back and arranged them again

steps.whatToRemember: The אנשי כנסת הגדולה created the order of the עמידה. When it was forgotten, שמעון הפקולי restored it.

phrases.english: They forgot them,
and he went back and arranged them again.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Historical reconciliation: two different stages in time
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two sources credit different people with arranging the same thing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The elders set the original order, and שמעון הפקולי restored it after it was forgotten.

steps.title: No adding praises beyond the fixed blessings
steps.stepSummary: After the fixed ברכות of שמונה עשרה, one may not add more praises of הקדוש ברוך הוא.
steps.simpleTranslation: From here on, it is forbidden to tell the praises of the Holy One, Blessed be He.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states a rule: the fixed ברכות are the limit, and we may not add extra praises of God to them. The next step gives the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier steps explained how the ברכות were set in order. Now the גמרא adds that this set wording is also a boundary. A person should not keep adding his own praises.

keyTerms.meaning: From here on; beyond this point
The Holy One, Blessed be He

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean you may never praise God. It means you may not stretch the fixed ברכות of the תפילה with extra praises beyond what the חכמים set.

phrases.english: From here on,
phrases.notes: Beyond the fixed blessings

phrases.aramaic: אָסוּר לְסַפֵּר בְּשִׁבְחוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא.
phrases.english: it is forbidden to tell the praise of the Holy One, Blessed be He.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the fixed order of the ברכות from steps 15-16 and adds that it may not be expanded
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not add more praises of God beyond the fixed ברכות.

steps.title: Only one who can say all of God's praise may speak it
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר reads a פסוק: only someone able to say all of God's praise should speak His mighty acts, and no one can.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי אלעזר said: What does the verse mean, 'Who can speak the mighty acts of ה׳, and make all His praise heard?' For whom is it fitting to speak ה׳'s mighty acts? For one who can make all His praise heard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source for the rule in step 17. רבי אלעזר explains a פסוק in תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק means only someone who could finish all of God's praise should start listing it. No person can do that. So we keep to the short set text of the חכמים instead of trying to list everything.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Elazar said,
What is the meaning of what is written:
"Who can speak the mighty acts of ה׳,
phrases.notes: תהלים קו:ב

phrases.english: and make all His praise heard?"
For whom is it fitting to speak the mighty acts of ה׳?
For one who can make all His praise heard.
phrases.notes: No one can, so we keep to the fixed text

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the פסוק behind the rule in step 17
steps.raayaObject: The ban on adding praises beyond the fixed ברכות
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים קו:ב as read by רבי אלעזר

steps.title: Over-praising God is dangerous
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that one who praises God too much is uprooted from the world, based on a פסוק in איוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: One who tells the praise of the Holy One, Blessed be He, too much is uprooted from the world, as it says: 'Can it be told to Him when I speak? If a man says it, he will be swallowed up.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא adds a stronger warning: over-praising God is not just improper, it brings punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 said it is not fitting to add praises. Here רבי יוחנן says the person is punished, because his long praise makes it look as if he could finish God's praise. The פסוק says such a man would be 'swallowed up'.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana said that Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: הַמְסַפֵּר בְּשִׁבְחוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
phrases.english: One who tells the praise of the Holy One, Blessed be He
too much —
is uprooted from the world,
as it says: "Can it be told to Him when I speak?
phrases.notes: איוב לז:כ

phrases.english: If a man says it, he will be swallowed up."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a punishment to the rule against extra praise
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Excessive praise of God brings the punishment of being uprooted from the world.

steps.title: Silence is the best praise
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה איש כפר גבוריא explains 'For You silence is praise': the best remedy of all is silence.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה of כפר גבוריא (some say of כפר גבור חיל) taught: What does the verse mean, 'For You, silence is praise'? The best remedy of all is silence.
steps.whatsHappening: Another חכם teaches a פסוק showing that the highest praise of God is quiet, not many words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 18-19 said what not to do: do not over-praise. This step says what is best: silence before God. Silence admits that God's greatness is beyond words.

keyTerms.meaning: The remedy for everything; the best medicine

phrases.aramaic: דָּרֵשׁ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אִישׁ כְּפַר גִּבּוֹרַיָּא,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda, a man of Kefar Gibboraya, taught,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ אִישׁ כְּפַר גִּבּוֹר חַיִל:
phrases.english: and some say he was a man of Kefar Gibbor Chayil:
phrases.notes: Two versions of his town's name

phrases.english: What is the meaning of what is written: "For You, silence is praise"?
phrases.notes: תהלים סה:ב

phrases.english: The best remedy of all is silence.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּרֵשׁ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אִישׁ כְּפַר גִּבּוֹרַיָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the warning against over-praise to the positive value of silence
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Silence is the best form of praise of God.

steps.title: A saying from ארץ ישראל: silence is worth double
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports a saying from ארץ ישראל: a word is worth a סלע, silence is worth two.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he said: In the West they say: A word is worth a סלע; silence is worth two.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a popular saying from ארץ ישראל that backs up the value of silence from the step before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a new rule. It is a well-known saying that supports רבי יהודה's teaching: silence is worth more than speech.

keyTerms.meaning: When he came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)
In the West, meaning ארץ ישראל

steps.whatToRemember: The fixed ברכות are the limit. Adding praise is improper (רבי אלעזר), even dangerous (רבי יוחנן), and silence is the best praise (רבי יהודה, רב דימי).

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came, he said:
They say in the West (Eretz Yisrael):
A word is worth a sela,
silence is worth two.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי, אֲמַר: אָמְרִי בְּמַעְרְבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 20 with a popular saying
steps.raayaObject: That silence is better than speech
steps.raayaSupportSource: A saying from ארץ ישראל reported by רב דימי

steps.title: Where do we learn that reading by heart does not count?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's rule that one who reads the מגילה by heart has not fulfilled his obligation, and asks for its source.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: If he read it by heart, he has not fulfilled his obligation. From where do we know this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It quotes the משנה about reading the מגילה by heart and asks where the rule comes from. This sets up רבא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the גמרא was on a side discussion about תפילה. Now it returns to the משנה. It wants a source showing the מגילה must be read from a written text.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know this?

phrases.aramaic: קְרָאָהּ עַל פֶּה לֹא יָצָא וְכוּ׳.
phrases.english: If one read it by heart, he has not fulfilled his obligation, etc.
phrases.notes: Quote from the משנה

phrases.english: From where do we know this?

steps.triggerLanguage: קְרָאָהּ עַל פֶּה לֹא יָצָא וְכוּ׳. מְנָלַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the תפילה discussion and returns to the משנה about reading the מגילה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that the מגילה must be read from a written text and not by heart

steps.title: Learning from עמלק: remembering means from a book
steps.stepSummary: רבא learns from a גזירה שוה of זכירה: as remembering עמלק is 'in the book', remembering the days of פורים must also be from a book.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: We learn it from 'remembering' and 'remembering'. Here it is written: 'And these days are remembered.' There it is written: 'Write this as a remembrance in the book.' Just as there it is in a book, so too here it is in a book.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question with a גזירה שוה, linking two פסוקים that share the word for remembering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מגילת אסתר says the days of פורים must be 'remembered'. The Torah says to write the remembrance of עמלק 'in the book'. Because the same word appears in both, the rule carries over: remembering פורים must also be from a written book, so reading by heart does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: Remembering; the shared word of the גזירה שוה
Just as there, so too here

steps.confusionAlert: The link is the shared word for remembering (נזכרים / זכרון). The words 'in the book' appear only in the עמלק פסוק and are carried over to the מגילה through that shared word.
steps.whatToRemember: The מגילה must be read from a written text. רבא learns this from a גזירה שוה with the remembrance of עמלק, which is 'in the book'.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is why we read the מגילה from a kosher written scroll and not from memory.

phrases.english: Rava said:
It is learned from 'remembering' and 'remembering',
phrases.notes: A גזירה שוה

phrases.english: It is written here: "And these days are remembered,"
phrases.notes: אסתר ט:כח

phrases.english: and it is written there: "Write this as a remembrance in the book."
phrases.notes: שמות יז:יד, about עמלק

phrases.english: Just as there, it is in a book,
so too here, it is in a book.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה of זכירה from עמלק ('in the book') shows the מגילה must be read from a written book.

steps.title: Maybe 'remembering' only means looking at the text
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא's גזירה שוה: why assume זכירה means reading aloud? Maybe silently looking at the text is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how do we know that this 'remembering' means reading aloud? Maybe it just means looking into the text.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts that the מגילה must come from a written text. It now asks whether you must actually say the words, or whether looking at them silently is enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's proof showed that the reading must be from a book, but it did not say how. Silently scanning a written text could also be called 'remembering from a book'. The גמרא wants a source showing the words must be spoken.

keyTerms.meaning: Looking into or scanning a text silently

phrases.english: And from where do we know that this 'remembering'
is reading aloud?
Perhaps it is merely looking into the text!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִמַּאי דְּהַאי זְכִירָה קְרִיאָה הִיא, דִּלְמָא עִיּוּן בְּעָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the scope of רבא's גזירה שוה from step 23
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that זכירה requires reading out loud
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'In the book' may only require seeing the text, not saying the words

steps.title: 'Remember' means with the mouth
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא proves that זָכוֹר means saying it out loud, because לֹא תִשְׁכָּח already covers remembering in the heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't think that. It is written 'Remember'. Could that mean in the heart? When it says 'Do not forget', forgetting from the heart is already covered. So how do I fulfill 'Remember'? With the mouth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the idea of silent reading. It brings a ברייתא showing that זָכוֹר must mean speaking the words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah gives two commands about עמלק: זָכוֹר and לֹא תִשְׁכָּח. Not forgetting already takes care of the heart. So זָכוֹר must add something new, which is saying it with the mouth. Through the גזירה שוה, the same applies to the מגילה.

keyTerms.meaning: It should not enter your mind; don't think that
In the heart, in one's thoughts

steps.whatToRemember: Reading the מגילה requires both a written text and saying the words aloud. Silent reading does not count.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basis for the rule that one must actually say or hear the words of the מגילה and of פרשת זכור.

phrases.english: It should not enter your mind
(as it is written): 'Remember.' Might it mean in the heart?
When it says 'You shall not forget,'
forgetting from the heart is already stated.
So how do I fulfill 'Remember'? With the mouth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Proof from a verse that otherwise would be extra (a ברייתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: זכירה might only mean looking at the text silently
steps.terutzMaskana: זכירה means saying the words out loud

steps.title: Why does the משנה need the translation rule?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about the משנה's rule that reading in תרגום does not count: if the text is in Hebrew, that is already the 'by heart' rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If he read it in translation he has not fulfilled his obligation.' What is the case? If it is written in the original Hebrew and he reads it in translation, that is the same as reading by heart!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next clause of the משנה. It asks what case this clause could mean, since one obvious reading would make it repeat the 'by heart' rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Translating Hebrew text aloud means you are not reading the words on the page. That is no different from saying them from memory, which the משנה already ruled out. So this clause would be redundant.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the circumstances?
The original Hebrew text of Tanach

phrases.english: If he read it in translation, he has not fulfilled his obligation, etc.
What is the case?
If you say it is written in the original Hebrew
and he reads it in translation,
that is the same as by heart!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִילֵּימָא דִּכְתִיבָה מִקְרָא וְקָרֵי לַהּ תַּרְגּוּם, הַיְינוּ עַל פֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next clause of the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's separate rule about reading in תרגום
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the text is Hebrew, translating it aloud is already covered by the 'by heart' rule, so the clause is redundant

steps.title: The מגילה is written in תרגום
steps.stepSummary: The rule is needed for a מגילה that is written in תרגום and read as written.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where it is written in translation and he reads it in translation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה means a מגילה that is actually written in Aramaic and read from that text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the person is reading from a written text, so the 'by heart' rule would not stop him. The משנה teaches that even so, a translated מגילה does not count. A new point is learned.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (the following case)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the problem is that he translated on the spot. He reads exactly what is written. The problem is that the written מגילה itself is in תרגום.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where it is written in translation and he reads it in translation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 26 by defining the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case is a Hebrew text read aloud in translation, which repeats the 'by heart' rule
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is a text written in תרגום, read as written

steps.title: Foreign language contradicts 'any language'
steps.stepSummary: The משנה allows reading in לעז for foreign speakers, but it also said reading in any language does not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'But we read it for foreign-language speakers in a foreign language, etc.' But you said: if he read it in any language, he has not fulfilled his obligation!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out an apparent contradiction inside the משנה about reading in other languages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One clause says no other language works. Another clause says foreign speakers may hear it in their language. Both cannot be true in the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: People who speak a foreign language

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל קוֹרִין אוֹתָהּ לַלּוֹעֲזוֹת בְּלַעַז וְכוּ׳.
phrases.english: But we read it for foreign-language speakers in a foreign language, etc.
But didn't you say:
If he read it in any language, he has not fulfilled his obligation!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אָמְרַתְּ: קְרָאָהּ בְּכׇל לָשׁוֹן — לֹא יָצָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next clause of the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's permission to read in לעז
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It seems to contradict the משנה's own rule that no other language counts

steps.title: רב and שמואל: only Greek
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל explain that the permitted foreign language is specifically Greek.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב and שמואל both say: in the Greek foreign language.
steps.whatsHappening: רב and שמואל resolve the contradiction by narrowing which foreign language the משנה allows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Any language' means languages in general, which do not count. 'לעז' means Greek specifically, which has a special status for translating the Torah. So the two clauses talk about different languages.

phrases.english: Rav and Shmuel, who both say:
In the Greek foreign language.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction in step 28
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of one clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: לעז means any foreign language, which would contradict 'any language does not count'

steps.title: Hebrew text read in Greek is 'by heart'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the Greek case is: if the text is in אשורית and read in Greek, that is reading by heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If it is written in אשורית and he reads it in Greek, that is the same as by heart!
steps.whatsHappening: Using the same question as before, the גמרא asks how reading in Greek could work if the מגילה is written in Hebrew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Translating a Hebrew text aloud into Greek is not reading what is written. That would be the 'by heart' case, which does not count. So the Greek permission needs a different case.

keyTerms.meaning: The Hebrew script and language in which Torah texts are written

phrases.english: What is the case?
If you say it is written in Ashurit (Hebrew)
and he reads it in Greek,
that is the same as by heart!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִילֵּימָא דִּכְתִיבָה אַשּׁוּרִית וְקָרֵי לַהּ יְווֹנִית, הַיְינוּ עַל פֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks the same kind of question as step 26 about the Greek ruling
steps.kashyaTarget: The case behind the Greek permission
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A Hebrew text translated aloud into Greek is reading by heart, which does not count

steps.title: The מגילה is written in Greek
steps.stepSummary: רבי אחא in the name of רבי אלעזר: the case is a מגילה written in Greek.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אחא said in the name of רבי אלעזר: it is written in the Greek foreign language.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the permission applies when the מגילה itself is written in Greek and read from that text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the person reads aloud from a written text, so it is not 'by heart'. Because Greek has special status, a מגילה written in Greek works for Greek speakers. This differs from a מגילה written in תרגום, which does not count.
steps.whatToRemember: At this stage: a valid reading must be aloud and from a written text, and a Hebrew text translated aloud counts as 'by heart'. The idea that the משנה allows only Greek is not final. Steps 36-39 revise it: any language counts for people who speak it, and Greek counts for everyone.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַחָא אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Acha said in the name of Rabbi Elazar:
That it is written in the Greek foreign language.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַחָא אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 30 by defining the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A Hebrew text is read aloud in Greek
steps.terutzMaskana: The מגילה is written in Greek and read as written

steps.title: God called יעקב by the name אל
steps.stepSummary: רבי אחא in the name of רבי אלעזר teaches that God called יעקב "אל", based on the פסוק "ויקרא לו אל אלהי ישראל".
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אחא said in the name of רבי אלעזר: Where do we see that God called יעקב "אל"? From the פסוק: "And he called him אל, the God of Israel."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second, unrelated teaching from the same rabbis it just quoted. It is a side point, not part of the מגילה discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 31 quoted רבי אחא in the name of רבי אלעזר, so the גמרא adds another teaching from the same pair. The claim is that the פסוק (בראשית ל״ג:כ) can be read as God calling יעקב "אל", not as יעקב naming the altar. The proof for this reading comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed be He (God)
A name of God, meaning a powerful one

steps.confusionAlert: This is a side teaching. It is quoted only because it comes from the same rabbis as the previous step. The מגילה discussion picks up again at מיתיבי.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אַחָא אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Acha said in the name of Rabbi Elazar:
From where do we know that the Holy One, Blessed be He, called
Jacob "El"?
As it says: "And he called him El, the God of Israel."
phrases.notes: בראשית ל״ג:כ. The simple reading is that יעקב named the altar.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אַחָא אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side teaching from the same rabbis quoted in step 31.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God gave יעקב the name "אל", as learned from בראשית ל״ג:כ.

steps.title: Proof from the missing name יעקב
steps.stepSummary: If יעקב had named the altar, the פסוק should have said "ויקרא לו יעקב". It does not, so יעקב is not the one doing the naming.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because if you think יעקב called the altar "אל", the פסוק should have said "And יעקב called it"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves its reading by pointing to a word that is missing from the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If יעקב were the one naming, we would expect his name to appear as the subject. Since it is missing, the speaker must be someone else, and יעקב is the one receiving the name.

keyTerms.meaning: Because if it enters your mind (if you think)

phrases.english: For if you were to think
that Jacob called the altar "El",
it should have said "And Jacob called it"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the reading claimed in step 32.
steps.raayaObject: That the פסוק describes God calling יעקב "אל".
steps.raayaSupportSource: The name יעקב is missing as the subject of "ויקרא".

steps.title: The correct reading of the verse
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק means: He called יעקב "אל". Who called him that? The God of Israel.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, "ויקרא לו" means He called יעקב "אל". And who called him "אל"? "The God of Israel."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the side teaching by rereading the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words "אלהי ישראל" are not part of the altar's name. They tell us who did the calling. So the פסוק reads: the God of Israel called יעקב "אל".

phrases.english: Rather, "and He called him," meaning Jacob, "El."
And who called him "El"?
"The God of Israel."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the proof in step 33.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The God of Israel called יעקב "אל".

steps.title: A ברייתא says reading in Greek does not count
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that reading the מגילה in Coptic, עברית, Elamite, Median or Greek does not count. This challenges רב ושמואל, who allowed Greek.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: If someone read it in Coptic, עברית, Elamite, Median or Greek, he has not fulfilled his obligation!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the מגילה and attacks רב ושמואל (step 29) with a ברייתא that lists Greek as not valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 29, רב ושמואל said the foreign language the משנה allows is Greek. This ברייתא names Greek among the languages that do not work, which seems to contradict them directly.

keyTerms.meaning: He has not fulfilled his obligation

phrases.english: They raised an objection: If he read it in Coptic, in Ivrit,
phrases.notes: "עברית" here is the script and language of those from across the river. It is not לשון הקודש.

phrases.english: in Elamite, Median, or Greek, he has not fulfilled his obligation!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side teaching and goes back to the Greek discussion of steps 29 to 31.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ושמואל's statement that Greek is the valid foreign language.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא explicitly lists Greek as not valid.

steps.title: Any language works for those who speak it
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is not like that ברייתא. It matches a different ברייתא: Coptic for Copts, Greek for Greeks, and so on, does count.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is only comparable to that: Coptic to Copts, עברית to עברים, Elamite to Elamites, Greek to Greeks, he has fulfilled his obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by bringing a second ברייתא. That ברייתא allows each language for the people who speak it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא is about reading to people who do not understand the language, and that does not count. The משנה's case of reading in a foreign language to its speakers matches the second ברייתא, where any language counts if the listeners understand it.

keyTerms.meaning: This is comparable only to that

steps.confusionAlert: The two ברייתות do not argue. The difference is the listener: a language you do not understand does not count, while your own language does.

phrases.english: This is comparable only to that:
Coptic to Copts, Ivrit to Ivrim,
Elamite to Elamites,
Greek to Greeks: he has fulfilled his obligation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the first ברייתא in step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing cases by citing a second ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first ברייתא rules out Greek completely.
steps.terutzMaskana: Any language, including Greek, counts when the listeners speak it. The first ברייתא is about non-speakers.

steps.title: Then why did רב and שמואל limit it to Greek?
steps.stepSummary: If any language works for its speakers, why did רב ושמואל explain the משנה as referring only to Greek? They should have said any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why did רב ושמואל explain our משנה as referring to Greek? Let them explain it as any foreign language!
steps.whatsHappening: The answer in step 36 creates a new problem. The גמרא now asks why רב ושמואל limited the משנה to Greek at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 36 said the משנה allows any foreign language to its speakers. That clashes with step 29, where רב ושמואל read the משנה as referring to Greek specifically. So their limiting explanation seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: They explain it as referring to (a case)

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי, רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל אַמַּאי מוֹקְמִי לַהּ
phrases.english: If so, why do Rav and Shmuel explain
our Mishnah as referring to the Greek language?
Let them explain it as any foreign language!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל אַמַּאי מוֹקְמִי לַהּ לְמַתְנִיתִין בְּלַעַז יְווֹנִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the result of step 36 against רב ושמואל's explanation in step 29.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ושמואל's explanation that the משנה refers to Greek.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the משנה allows every language for its speakers, limiting it to Greek makes no sense.

steps.title: רב and שמואל's statement was a separate rule
steps.stepSummary: The משנה follows the ברייתא and allows any language for its speakers. רב ושמואל's statement was not an explanation of the משנה. It was a separate, general rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, our משנה is like the ברייתא. And what was said by רב ושמואל was said as a general statement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by separating the two. The משנה is one thing, and רב ושמואל's statement is another. It sets up the actual wording of their rule in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא withdraws the idea from step 29 that רב ושמואל were explaining the משנה. The משנה matches the second ברייתא: any language for its speakers. רב ושמואל taught their own independent rule about Greek.

keyTerms.meaning: It was said as a general, stand-alone statement

phrases.english: [Rather, our Mishnah is like the baraita.]
And when the statement of Rav and Shmuel was said,
it was said as a general statement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 37.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the statement: it is not an explanation of the משנה but an independent rule.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב ושמואל were limiting the משנה to Greek.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה allows any language for its speakers. רב ושמואל taught a separate rule.

steps.title: Greek is valid for everyone
steps.stepSummary: רב ושמואל both say: the Greek language is valid for everyone, even for someone who does not understand Greek.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ושמואל both say: The Greek language is valid for everyone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states רב ושמואל's actual rule. Greek has a special status for reading the מגילה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Other languages count only for people who understand them. Greek counts for everyone, even someone who does not speak it. This explains why Greek was singled out.
steps.whatToRemember: There are three levels. Any foreign language counts for people who speak it. A foreign language you do not understand does not count. Greek is special: it counts for everyone, even non-speakers. (The original Hebrew always counts, even without understanding, as steps 44-47 show.)
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets out the rules for reading the מגילה in translation. It also shows that Greek has a unique standing among foreign languages.

phrases.english: Rav and Shmuel, who both said:
The Greek language is valid for everyone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the wording of the general rule mentioned in step 38.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Reading the מגילה in Greek is valid for everyone, even those who do not understand Greek.

steps.title: The ברייתא seems to limit Greek to Greeks only
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב ושמואל: the ברייתא says 'Greek for Greeks,' which implies Greek does not work for everyone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the ברייתא teaches: Greek for Greeks. For Greeks, yes. For everyone, no!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב ושמואל's rule from Step 39. They said Greek works for everyone, but the ברייתא only allows Greek for Greeks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא from Step 36 says 'Coptic for Copts, Greek for Greeks.' Read carefully, this means Greek works only for people who speak Greek. That contradicts רב ושמואל, who said Greek works even for someone who does not understand it.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches (introduces what a ברייתא or משנה says)

phrases.english: But doesn't it teach:
Greek for Greeks — for Greeks, yes,
phrases.notes: The second 'for Greeks,' in square brackets, is part of the corrected wording; some versions don't have it.

phrases.english: for everyone else — no!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule of רב ושמואל stated in Step 39.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ושמואל's rule that Greek is valid for everyone
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's wording 'Greek for Greeks' implies Greek is invalid for non-Greeks. This directly contradicts רב ושמואל.

steps.title: רב ושמואל follow רבן שמעון בן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: רב ושמואל hold like רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who says that even ספרים may be written only in Greek, so Greek has a special status.
steps.simpleTranslation: They (רב ושמואל) said their rule following רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. As we learned in a משנה: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: Even for ספרים, they only permitted them to be written in Greek.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב ושמואל do not follow that ברייתא. They follow רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that ספרי תנ"ך may be written in Greek, but in no other foreign language. This shows that Greek is treated almost like the original Hebrew. So for רב ושמואל, Greek is not just a translation for Greek speakers. It is valid for everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: They said it according to (they follow the opinion of)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that Greek is not just one translation among many. It has a unique standing in הלכה.

phrases.aramaic: אִינְהוּ דַּאֲמוּר כְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל.
phrases.english: They spoke in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

phrases.aramaic: דִּתְנַן, רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: As we learned in a mishna, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה in מגילה ח:

phrases.english: Even for books of Scripture, they did not permit
that they be written in any language except Greek.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינְהוּ דַּאֲמוּר כְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 40.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attribution to a different תנא (the opinions are a dispute between תנאים)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רב ושמואל had to fit the ברייתא that limits Greek to Greeks.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב ושמואל follow רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, for whom Greek has special status and works for everyone.

steps.title: Why not just say the הלכה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל?
steps.stepSummary: If רב ושמואל follow רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, they should have simply said 'the הלכה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let them say: the הלכה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the way רב ושמואל worded their statement. Why make a new rule instead of just ruling like an existing opinion?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually an אמורא who agrees with a תנא simply says 'the הלכה follows him.' Stating it as a fresh rule looks unnecessary. The גמרא wants to know what extra lesson their wording teaches.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֵימְרוּ: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל?
phrases.english: Then let them say: The halakha is in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵימְרוּ: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of רב ושמואל in light of the answer in Step 41.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrasing of רב ושמואל's statement
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If they only agree with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, a simple 'the הלכה follows him' would have been enough. A new formulation seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Their own wording teaches that it applies even to מגילה
steps.stepSummary: A plain 'the הלכה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל' might seem to cover only other ספרים, not מגילה, which has the word 'ככתבם.' So רב ושמואל stated it outright for מגילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they had said 'the הלכה follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל,' I would have thought: that is only for other ספרים. But a מגילה, about which it is written 'ככתבם' (according to their writing), I would say Greek does not work. So they teach us that it does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that רב ושמואל's special wording adds something new. Their rule applies even to מגילה, despite the word 'ככתבם.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says the מגילה must be read 'ככתבם,' according to how it is written. That might suggest the original language is required. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל spoke about ספרים in general, so ruling like him might not cover מגילה. By stating their rule directly about מגילה, רב ושמואל show that Greek works even here.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have thought (an initial, mistaken assumption)

steps.whatToRemember: רב ושמואל: Greek is valid for מגילה for everyone. This follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, and it holds even though the פסוק says 'ככתבם.'

phrases.aramaic: אִי אָמְרִי הֲלָכָה כְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל,
phrases.english: Had they said the halakha is in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה אָמֵינָא הָנֵי מִילֵּי שְׁאָר סְפָרִים,
phrases.english: I would have said this applies only to other books,
but the Megilla, about which it is written 'according to their writing' —
I would say it does not (work in Greek).
So they teach us (that it does).

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי אָמְרִי הֲלָכָה כְּרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording question in Step 42.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A הוה אמינא that the special wording comes to prevent
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A plain ruling like רבן שמעון בן גמליאל would cover only other ספרים, not מגילה, because of 'ככתבם.'
steps.terutzMaskana: רב ושמואל's own wording teaches that Greek is valid even for מגילה.

steps.title: How can a לועז fulfill the מצוה without understanding Hebrew?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that a לועז who hears the מגילה in אשורית is יוצא, and asks: he does not understand what is being said!
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: a לועז who heard it in אשורית has fulfilled his obligation. But he does not know what they are saying!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now moves to a new line in the משנה. It quotes the line, then challenges it: how can someone be יוצא if he does not understand the words?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, the discussion allowed other languages so that people could understand. That suggests understanding matters. If so, a לועז who hears only Hebrew he cannot follow should not be יוצא.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who speaks only a foreign language
The Hebrew script and language of the מגילה

phrases.english: And one who speaks a foreign language who heard it in Ashurit has fulfilled his obligation, etc.
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה, which opens a new topic.

phrases.english: But doesn't he not know what they are saying?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next clause of the משנה. This begins a new topic.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that a לועז who hears אשורית is יוצא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Fulfilling the מצוה seems to require understanding, and the לועז does not understand Hebrew.

steps.title: Just like נשים and עמי הארץ
steps.stepSummary: The לועז is like נשים and עמי הארץ, who also understand little Hebrew yet are יוצא when they hear the מגילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is just like women and unlearned people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by comparing the לועז to people who are clearly יוצא. נשים and עמי הארץ often do not understand Hebrew, yet they fulfill the מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees that נשים and עמי הארץ are יוצא with a Hebrew reading. So understanding cannot be a strict requirement. The לועז is the same.

phrases.english: It is just as with women and uneducated people.
phrases.notes: אַנָּשִׁים here means 'with women' (אַ = עַל + נָשִׁים), not 'men.'

steps.confusionAlert: אַנָּשִׁים here does NOT mean 'men.' It is a contraction of 'אַ נָשִׁים,' meaning 'like the case of women.'
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 44.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought that not understanding the words makes the reading invalid for the listener.
steps.terutzMaskana: נשים and עמי הארץ do not understand either, yet they are יוצא. So is the לועז.

steps.title: רבינא: even scholars don't understand every word
steps.stepSummary: רבינא objects: do even we scholars understand words like 'האחשתרנים בני הרמכים'? So the whole question assumes something false.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא objected: Is that to say that we know what 'האחשתרנים בני הרמכים' means?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא attacks the starting assumption of the question in Step 44. He points out that even learned people do not understand every word of the מגילה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumed that someone who does not understand the words cannot be יוצא. רבינא shows this cannot be right. Even the חכמים do not know the meaning of rare words in the מגילה, and yet no one doubts that they are יוצא. So the comparison to נשים is not even needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Obscure words in אסתר ח:י (royal steeds / bred from the stud)

phrases.english: Ravina strongly objects to it:
Is that to say that we — 'ha'aḥashteranim benei haramakhim' —
do we know (what it means)?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption behind the question in Step 44, making the answer in Step 45 unnecessary.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The premise of the question, that understanding is required to be יוצא
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Even scholars do not understand every word of the מגילה, yet they are certainly יוצא.

steps.title: The מצוה is reading and publicizing the miracle
steps.stepSummary: We are יוצא through מצות קריאה and פרסומי ניסא even without understanding every word. The same is true for the לועז.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is the מצוה of reading and publicizing the miracle. Here too, it is the מצוה of reading and publicizing the miracle.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא finishes his point and gives the real reason the לועז is יוצא. The מצוה is the reading itself and publicizing the miracle, not understanding each word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The scholars are יוצא without understanding rare words because the reading itself is the מצוה, and it spreads the story of the miracle. The same reasoning applies to the לועז hearing Hebrew. The original Hebrew reading fulfills both קריאה and פרסומי ניסא, whether or not the listener understands.
steps.whatToRemember: Hearing the מגילה in its original Hebrew fulfills the מצוה even if you do not understand it. The מצוה is the reading and פרסומי ניסא, not understanding every word.
steps.whyThisMatters: This defines what the מצוה of מגילה really is. That is why people today who do not understand Hebrew are still יוצא by hearing the Hebrew reading.

phrases.english: Rather, it is the מצוה of reading and publicizing the miracle,

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי — מִצְוַת קְרִיאָה וּפַרְסוֹמֵי נִיסָּא.
phrases.english: here too — it is the מצוה of reading and publicizing the miracle.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבינא's objection by giving the true reason the לועז is יוצא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A לועז who hears the מגילה in Hebrew is יוצא, because the מצוה consists of the reading and פרסומי ניסא, not comprehension.

steps.title: The משנה's phrase: reading the מגילה 'סירוגין'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next phrase of the משנה: if someone reads the מגילה סירוגין, he is יוצא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if he read it 'סירוגין', he has fulfilled his obligation, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new phrase in the משנה about reading the מגילה. This line is a setup for the next question: what does סירוגין mean?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion about the לועז is finished. Now the גמרא quotes a new ruling from the משנה. The ruling uses a rare word, and the next lines explain that word.

keyTerms.meaning: With breaks, a little at a time
And so on (the quote continues in the משנה)

phrases.english: If he read it at intervals, he has fulfilled his obligation, etc.
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה. It opens the new topic.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. The discussion of the לועז has ended, and the גמרא quotes the next phrase of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who reads the מגילה סירוגין is יוצא.

steps.title: The רבנן did not know the word 'סירוגין'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reports that the רבנן did not know what סירוגין means.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן did not know what 'סירוגין' means.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells us the רבנן were unsure what this word in the משנה means. This sets up the next step, where they find out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line is written as a story, but it works like a question about the meaning of a word. You cannot apply the law until you know what סירוגין means.

phrases.english: The Sages did not know what 'seirugin' means.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what the key word in the משנה just quoted means.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the word סירוגין.

steps.title: The maidservant explains 'סירוגין' without meaning to
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן heard the maidservant of רבי scold them for coming in a few at a time: 'How long will you come in סירוגין סירוגין?' So סירוגין means with breaks.
steps.simpleTranslation: They heard the maidservant of the house of רבי. The רבנן were coming into the house of רבי in small groups. She said to them: 'How long will you keep coming in סירוגין סירוגין?'
steps.whatsHappening: The answer comes from daily life. The maidservant used the word for people coming in a few at a time. That told the רבנן that סירוגין means 'with breaks in between'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The maidservant lived in the house of רבי, where pure Hebrew was spoken, so her speech counted as good evidence for what the word means. Applied to our משנה: someone who reads the מגילה with pauses in between is still יוצא.

keyTerms.meaning: The maidservant of the house of רבי (רבי יהודה הנשיא)
In groups, a few at a time

steps.confusionAlert: סירוגין does not mean reading the verses out of order. It means reading in the correct order but stopping and starting, with breaks in between.

phrases.english: They heard the maidservant of Rabbi's house
saying to the Sages

phrases.aramaic: דַּהֲווֹ עָיְילִי פִּסְקֵי פִּסְקֵי לְבֵי רַבִּי:
phrases.english: who were entering Rabbi's house a few at a time:

phrases.aramaic: עַד מָתַי אַתֶּם נִכְנָסִין סֵירוּגִין סֵירוּגִין?
phrases.english: How long will you keep entering at intervals?
phrases.notes: From the way she used the word, they learned that סירוגין means 'with breaks'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about what סירוגין means.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: סירוגין means at intervals, with breaks in between.
steps.whyThisMatters: This defines the הלכה: reading the מגילה with pauses still counts.

steps.title: The רבנן did not know the word 'חלוגלוגות'
steps.stepSummary: A second example: the רבנן did not know what חלוגלוגות means.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן did not know what 'חלוגלוגות' means.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives more cases where the רבנן learned a word from the same maidservant. This line sets up the next word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This word is not from our משנה. It appears in other משניות and ברייתות. The גמרא groups these word-learning stories together because they all work the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: A plant mentioned in משניות. It turns out to mean purslane.

phrases.english: The Sages did not know what 'chalogelogot' means.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same pattern as before for a new word.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the word חלוגלוגות.

steps.title: The maidservant reveals that 'חלוגלוגות' is purslane
steps.stepSummary: The maidservant scolded a man who was scattering purslane: 'How long will you scatter your חלוגלוגות?' So חלוגלוגות is purslane.
steps.simpleTranslation: They heard the maidservant of the house of רבי. A man was scattering purslane, and she said to him: 'How long will you scatter your חלוגלוגות?'
steps.whatsHappening: Once again, the maidservant's everyday words show what the word means. She called the purslane חלוגלוגות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man was scattering פרפחיני, which is purslane, and she called it חלוגלוגות. This showed the רבנן that the two words name the same plant.

phrases.english: They heard the maidservant of Rabbi's house
who said to a certain man
who was scattering purslane:
How long will you keep scattering your chalogelogot?
phrases.notes: This shows that חלוגלוגות means purslane.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about what חלוגלוגות means.

steps.title: The רבנן did not know 'סלסלה' in the verse
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן did not know what סלסלה means in the פסוק in משלי: 'סלסלה ותרוממך'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן did not know what 'סלסלה, and it will raise you up' means.
steps.whatsHappening: Now a word from a פסוק in משלי, about getting wisdom, is unclear to the רבנן. This sets up the next story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same method is used here to explain a word in תנ"ך, not only a word in a משנה. Everyday speech helps explain a פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: A word in משלי about wisdom, meaning still unclear here
And it will raise you up

phrases.aramaic: לָא הֲווֹ יָדְעִי רַבָּנַן מַאי ״סַלְסְלֶהָ וּתְרוֹמְמֶךָּ״.
phrases.english: The Sages did not know what 'salseleha, and it will exalt you' means.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא הֲווֹ יָדְעִי רַבָּנַן מַאי ״סַלְסְלֶהָ וּתְרוֹמְמֶךָּ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The same pattern, now applied to a word in a פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of סלסלה in משלי.

steps.title: The maidservant reveals 'סלסלה' means turning over
steps.stepSummary: The maidservant told a man who kept twirling his hair: 'How long will you מסלסל your hair?' So סלסלה means to turn something over and over.
steps.simpleTranslation: They heard the maidservant of the house of רבי. She was talking to a man who kept twirling his hair, and she said to him: 'How long will you keep twirling your hair?'
steps.whatsHappening: From her words, the רבנן learned that סלסל means to turn something around again and again. So the פסוק means: keep turning wisdom over, and it will raise you up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man was twirling his hair, and she called this מסלסל. Applied to the פסוק, it means you should review and turn over the Torah again and again, and that is what lifts a person up.

phrases.english: They heard the maidservant of Rabbi's house
who was speaking to a certain man
who was twirling his hair,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ: עַד מָתַי אַתָּה מְסַלְסֵל בִּשְׂעָרְךָ?
phrases.english: she said to him: How long will you keep twirling your hair?
phrases.notes: This shows that סלסל means to turn around and around.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about what סלסלה means.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: סלסלה means turn it (wisdom) over and over.

steps.title: The רבנן did not know 'יהבך' in the verse
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן did not know what יהבך means in the פסוק in תהלים: 'השלך על ה׳ יהבך'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן did not know what 'Cast your יהב upon ה׳' means.
steps.whatsHappening: Another unclear word, this time in a פסוק in תהלים. This sets up a story from a different source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the answer will not come from the maidservant. It will come from a story told by an אמורא.

phrases.aramaic: לָא הֲווֹ יָדְעִי רַבָּנַן מַאי: ״הַשְׁלֵךְ עַל ה׳ יְהָבְךָ״.
phrases.english: The Sages did not know what 'Cast your yehav upon the Lord' means.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא הֲווֹ יָדְעִי רַבָּנַן מַאי: ״הַשְׁלֵךְ עַל ה׳ יְהָבְךָ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The same pattern, now for a word in תהלים.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of יהבך in תהלים.

steps.title: An Arab traveler shows that 'יהב' means a burden
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה was traveling with an Arab and carrying a load. The Arab said: 'Take your יהב and throw it on my camel.' So יהב means a burden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said: Once I was traveling with a certain Arab, and I was carrying a load. He said to me: 'Take your יהב and throw it on my camel.'
steps.whatsHappening: The Arab called the load a 'יהב'. That showed רבה בר בר חנה what the word means. The פסוק means: throw your burden onto ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the meaning comes from a related language spoken by an outsider, not from the house of רבי. The point is the same: everyday speech can explain a rare word in תנ"ך. Here the פסוק teaches a person to hand his heavy burdens over to ה׳.
steps.whatToRemember: The רבנן sometimes learned the meaning of rare words from everyday speech: the maidservant of רבי, and an Arab traveler. סירוגין means with breaks, חלוגלוגות means purslane, סלסלה means turn it over and over, and יהב means a burden.

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana said:
One time I was traveling
with a certain Arab,
and I was carrying a load

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַר לִי: שְׁקוֹל יַהְבָּיךְ וּשְׁדִי אַגַּמְלַאי.
phrases.english: and he said to me: Take your yehav and throw it on my camel.
phrases.notes: He used yehav for the load, so the word means a burden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה: זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה אָזֵילְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about what יהבך means.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: יהב means a burden or load.

steps.title: The רבנן did not know the meaning of 'מטאטא'
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן did not know what the words 'וטאטאתיה במטאטא השמד' in ישעיה mean.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן did not know what is meant by: 'וטאטאתיה במטאטא השמד' ('And I will sweep it with the broom of destruction').
steps.whatsHappening: This is one more case in the same list: the רבנן did not understand a rare word in a פסוק. The next line will give the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in ישעיה 14:23 describes how בבל will be destroyed, but the words טאטאתיה and מטאטא were unclear. Like the earlier cases (סלסלה, יהבך), the answer will come from everyday speech, not from a scholar.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And I will tatei it' – the unclear verb in the פסוק
The unclear noun in the פסוק (later: a broom)

phrases.english: The Sages did not know
phrases.notes: This opens the same way as the earlier stories in this list.

phrases.english: what is meant by: 'And I will tatei it with the matatei of destruction.'
phrases.notes: ישעיה 14:23, about the destruction of בבל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of rare words the רבנן learned from ordinary speech.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of טאטאתיה and מטאטא in the פסוק.

steps.title: The maidservant tells her friend to sweep the house
steps.stepSummary: They heard רבי's maidservant say: 'Take the טאטיתא and sweep the house,' so מטאטא means a broom.
steps.simpleTranslation: They heard the maidservant of רבי's house saying to her friend: 'Take the broom (טאטיתא) and sweep (טאטי) the house.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the answer: the maidservant used these words in daily housework. From her words the רבנן learned that מטאטא is a broom and טאטא means to sweep.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The maidservant used the same root in two ways: the noun (טאטיתא, the broom) and the verb (טאטי, sweep). So the פסוק means: 'I will sweep בבל away with the broom of destruction.'
steps.whatToRemember: This ends the list of words the רבנן learned from everyday speech, mostly from רבי's maidservant. מטאטא = broom; טאטא = to sweep.

phrases.english: They heard the maidservant of Rabbi's house
who was saying to her friend:
Take the broom and sweep the house.
phrases.notes: Noun and verb from the same root as in the פסוק.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 57.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: מטאטא is a broom and טאטא means to sweep, learned from how the maidservant spoke.

steps.title: Reading the מגילה with breaks is valid
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches: if someone read the מגילה in סירוגין (with breaks), he has fulfilled his obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If one read it (the מגילה) at intervals, he has fulfilled his obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the הלכות of reading the מגילה and quotes a ברייתא. Its first rule is that reading with pauses still counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: סירוגין means reading part, stopping, and later going on from where he stopped. The ברייתא says these breaks do not ruin the reading, so he is יוצא.

keyTerms.meaning: With breaks: stopping and later continuing

steps.confusionAlert: סירוגין does NOT mean reading out of order (that is called למפרע). It means reading in the correct order, but with pauses in between.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical הלכה: someone who must stop in the middle of the מגילה reading does not have to start over.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
If one read it at intervals, he has fulfilled his obligation,
phrases.notes: The ברייתא continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the list of rare words and returns to the סירוגין clause of the משנה (steps 48-50), now quoting a ברייתא about it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Reading the מגילה with pauses (סירוגין) is valid; the reader is יוצא.
